Proofs of some OEIS conjectures on Wythoff sums,
Fibonacci and Lucas words

Alex Ashburn Address: Independent Researcher Email address: aashburn1998@gmail.com
Abstract.

We prove several conjectures from the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences about the lower and upper Wythoff sequences and the Fibonacci word. Among them are two of Kimberling’s three conjectures on the number of ways to write n=⌊h​φ⌋+⌊k​φ2⌋n=\lfloor h\varphi\rfloor+\lfloor k\varphi^{2}\rfloor with h,k≥1h,k\geq 1 (A259598): exactly one way if and only if n+1=2​Fn+1=2F for a Fibonacci number F≥2F\geq 2, and exactly two ways if and only if n+1≥7n+1\geq 7 is a Lucas number. The third conjecture, that no way exists if and only if n+1n+1 is a Fibonacci number, was proved earlier by Kawsumarng et al. We also observe that Kimberling’s conjecture on the gaps of the sums of two distinct terms of A003622 and of their complement (A333308, A333309) follows, after a shift by 22, from earlier Walnut results of Shallit and of Bosma et al. on A260317, and we re-verify it. Next, we prove Kimberling’s five 2025 conjectures on the gaps between positions where the Fibonacci word and the “Lucas word” take prescribed values (A383423–A383427). Finally, we prove a conjecture of Mathar on A285383, and we point out that a conjecture of Schmidt on A003250 follows from theorems of Carlitz, Scoville and Vaughan (1973); we also confirm it with Walnut. Most proofs are decision procedures run in the free prover Walnut, and we supply the complete command file.

Key words and phrases: 
Wythoff sequences, Fibonacci word, Lucas word, Zeckendorf representation, automatic sequences, Walnut, OEIS
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
11B85, 68R15, 11B39, 03B25

1. Introduction

Let φ=(1+5)/2\varphi=(1+\sqrt{5})/2. The lower and upper Wythoff sequences are u⁡(n)=⌊n​φ⌋u(n)=\left\lfloor n\varphi\right\rfloor (A000201) and v⁡(n)=⌊n​φ2⌋=u⁡(n)+nv(n)=\left\lfloor n\varphi^{2}\right\rfloor=u(n)+n (A001950). The Fibonacci word 𝐟=f0f1f2⋯=0100101001001⋯\mathbf{f}=f_{0}f_{1}f_{2}\cdots=0100101001001\cdots (A003849) is the fixed point of 0↦010\mapsto 01, 1↦01\mapsto 0. The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences [7] records many conjectures about these objects, several of them due to Clark Kimberling. In this note we prove the following, which were listed as conjectures in the OEIS as of September 2026.

  1. (1)

    A259598 (Kimberling, 2015). Let r⁡(n)r(n) be the number of pairs (h,k)(h,k) with h,k≥1h,k\geq 1 and n=u⁡(h)+v⁡(k)n=u(h)+v(k). Kimberling conjectured the following:

    1. (a)

      r⁡(n)=0r(n)=0 iff n∈{1,2,4,7,12,…}={F−1:F≥2​ a Fibonacci number}n\in\{1,2,4,7,12,\dots\}=\{F-1:F\geq 2\text{ a Fibonacci number}\};

    2. (b)

      r⁡(n)=1r(n)=1 iff n∈{3,5,9,15,25,41,…}n\in\{3,5,9,15,25,41,\dots\} (the terms ≥3\geq 3 of A001595);

    3. (c)

      r⁡(n)=2r(n)=2 iff n∈{6,10,17,28,46,…}n\in\{6,10,17,28,46,\dots\} (the terms ≥6\geq 6 of A001610).

    Part (a) was proved by Kawsumarng, Khemaratchatakumthorn, Noppakaew and Pongsriiam [5], and reproved with Walnut by Shallit [10]. We prove (b) and (c).

  2. (2)

    A333308, A333309 (Kimberling, 2020). Let SS be the set of sums of two distinct terms of A003622 ={v⁡(n)−1:n≥1}=\{v(n)-1:n\geq 1\}. Conjecture: the difference sequences of SS and of its complement {1,2,3,…}∖S\{1,2,3,\dots\}\setminus S consist of Fibonacci numbers. The gap sets are exactly {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\} and {1,2,3,5}\{1,2,3,5\}. This is not new: S+2S+2 is the set of sums of two distinct upper Wythoff numbers, whose complement is A260317, so the statement follows from Shallit’s Walnut proof that the gaps of A260317 are exactly 1,2,3,51,2,3,5 [9] and from a lemma of Bosma et al. [1]; see Section 4.

  3. (3)

    A383423–A383427 (Kimberling, 2025). Five conjectures on the gaps between the positions kk at which (fk,ℓk)(f_{k},\ell_{k}) takes a given value, where ℓ\boldsymbol{\ell} is the Lucas word A383422.

  4. (4)

    A003250 (Schmidt, 2014): a⁡(n)=⌊(3−φ)​A003234​(n)⌋a(n)=\left\lfloor(3-\varphi)\,\mathrm{A003234}(n)\right\rfloor. This is not new: it follows in one line from a formula that Schmidt recorded in the same entry, which rests on theorems of Carlitz, Scoville and Vaughan [3]. We include it with an independent automata check.

  5. (5)

    A285383 (Mathar, 2017): the limiting 00-word of the morphism 0↦110\mapsto 11, 1↦011\mapsto 01 is 00 followed by the period-doubling sequence A035263.

We found no proofs of items (1b), (1c), (3) or (5) in the OEIS entries, their cross-references, or the literature we searched, which included [5, 10, 8, 1]. All but the last are statements in first-order logic over ⟨ℕ,+⟩\langle\mathbb{N},+\rangle extended by Fibonacci-automatic predicates. By a theorem of Bruyère and Hansel [2], which extends the classical results for integer bases to numeration systems such as Zeckendorf’s (see also [11, 8]), such statements are decidable, and we decide them with Walnut [6, 11]. The command file walnut_proofs.txt is posted together with this paper. We ran it with the development version 8.0-alpha of Walnut (commit 49a16a3 of https://github.com/Walnut-Theorem-Prover/Walnut, September 2026), from the Walnut home directory, as java -jar target/Walnut-all.jar < walnut_proofs.txt; it takes a few seconds. The latest tagged version, Walnut 7.1 (tag v7.1.0, whose jar file is build/libs/Walnut-all.jar), gives the same results.

2. Method

Every n≥0n\geq 0 has a unique Zeckendorf representation as a sum of non-adjacent Fibonacci numbers FjF_{j} with j≥2j\geq 2. Walnut’s numeration system msd_fib reads these representations most significant digit first. The Fibonacci word is available in Walnut as the automatic word F, with F​[i]=fi\texttt{F}[i]=f_{i}.

We use the classical fact that the lower Wythoff sequence is Fibonacci-synchronized. If shift⁡(m)\mathrm{shift}(m) denotes the number whose Zeckendorf representation is that of mm followed by a 00, then

(1) u⁡(n)=shift⁡(n−1)+1(n≥1).u(n)=\mathrm{shift}(n-1)+1\qquad(n\geq 1).

This is well known (see, e.g., [11, Ch. 10] and [4]). We also checked it directly for all n≤105n\leq 10^{5}. In Walnut, (1) becomes

reg shift msd_fib msd_fib "([0,0]|([0,1][1,1]*[1,0]))*";
def phin "?msd_fib (n=0 & x=0) | (n>=1 & Ey $shift(n-1,y) & x=y+1)";
def phi2n "?msd_fib Ey $phin(n,y) & x=y+n";

so that phin(n,x) holds iff x=u⁡(n)x=u(n) and phi2n(n,x) holds iff x=v⁡(n)x=v(n). The command file checks that phin defines a total function with the correct first values. The Fibonacci numbers are the integers whose Zeckendorf representation matches 0*10*. The Lucas numbers Lj=Fj−1+Fj+1L_{j}=F_{j-1}+F_{j+1} with j≥3j\geq 3 (that is, 4,7,11,18,…4,7,11,18,\dots) are those matching 0*1010*; we only use Lucas numbers ≥7\geq 7.

For each statement, we write a first-order formula and have Walnut decide it. Each gap statement has the form “y−x∈Dy-x\in D for every pair x<yx<y of consecutive elements of XX, and every d∈Dd\in D occurs”. As a guard against encoding mistakes, the file also evaluates deliberately false variants of two of the gap statements (a333308_gaps_false and a383423_false, each with one gap value removed), and Walnut returns FALSE for both.

3. Representations as lower plus upper Wythoff numbers

Theorem 1.

Let r(n)=#{(h,k):h,k≥1,u(h)+v(k)=n}r(n)=\#\{(h,k):h,k\geq 1,\ u(h)+v(k)=n\}. For n≥1n\geq 1:

  1. (a)

    r⁡(n)=0r(n)=0 iff n+1n+1 is a Fibonacci number ≥2\geq 2 ([5]);

  2. (b)

    r⁡(n)=1r(n)=1 iff n+1=2​Fn+1=2F for a Fibonacci number F≥2F\geq 2;

  3. (c)

    r⁡(n)=2r(n)=2 iff n+1n+1 is a Lucas number ≥7\geq 7.

Proof.

With rep(h,k,n) expressing h,k≥1h,k\geq 1 and n=u⁡(h)+v⁡(k)n=u(h)+v(k), Walnut returns TRUE for

An (n>=1) => ($one(n) <=> (Ef $isfib(f) & f>=2 & n+1=2*f))
An (n>=1) => ($two(n) <=> ($islucas(n+1) & n+1>=7))

where one and two express “exactly one” and “exactly two” representations in first-order terms (see the command file). Walnut also confirms (a). ∎

Since 2​Fj−12F_{j}-1 runs through 3,5,9,15,25,41,…3,5,9,15,25,41,\dots (A001595 for j≥3j\geq 3) and Lj−1L_{j}-1 through 6,10,17,28,46,…6,10,17,28,46,\dots (A001610 for j≥4j\geq 4), this settles Kimberling’s conjectures.

4. Sums of two distinct terms of A003622

A003622 ={1,4,6,9,12,14,…}={v⁡(n)−1:n≥1}=\{1,4,6,9,12,14,\dots\}=\{v(n)-1:n\geq 1\} is the set of positive integers whose Zeckendorf representation ends in 11. Let SS (A333308) be the set of sums of two distinct elements of A003622, and let C={1,2,3,…}∖SC=\{1,2,3,\dots\}\setminus S (A333309). Since vv is increasing, S={v⁡(m)+v⁡(n)−2:1≤m<n}=T−2S=\{v(m)+v(n)-2:1\leq m<n\}=T-2, where T={v⁡(m)+v⁡(n):1≤m<n}T=\{v(m)+v(n):1\leq m<n\} is the set of sums of two distinct upper Wythoff numbers; TT contains no integer below 77. The complement of TT in the positive integers is A260317, so

C={y−2:y∈A260317,y≥3}.C=\{y-2:\ y\in\mathrm{A260317},\ y\geq 3\}.
Theorem 2.

The set of differences of consecutive elements of SS is exactly {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\}. The set of differences of consecutive elements of CC is exactly {1,2,3,5}\{1,2,3,5\}. In particular, both difference sequences consist of Fibonacci numbers, as Kimberling conjectured.

Proof.

Walnut decides the statements a333308_gaps and a333309_gaps in the command file. Each asserts that every gap lies in the given set and that every element of the set occurs as a gap. Both return TRUE. Removing 33 from the first set gives FALSE. ∎

Remark 3.

Theorem 2 is a translate of known results. By the identity above, the gaps of CC are the terms of A260311 (the gaps of A260317) after its first two terms, which are both 11. Shallit [9] proved with Walnut that every gap of A260317 lies in {1,2,3,5}\{1,2,3,5\} (all four occur) (see also his comments in A260317 and A260311, and [1]), and the gap 11 occurs again later in A260311 (for example as its tenth term); this gives the second statement. The gaps of SS are those of TT, and two consecutive elements of TT differ by 11 plus the number of elements of A260317 between them. Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl and Tromp [1, Lemma 1] proved that the tenth gap of A260317 is the last one equal to 11, so no two consecutive integers ≥14\geq 14 both lie in A260317, and consecutive elements t<t′t<t^{\prime} of TT with t≥13t\geq 13 differ by 11 or 22. Since TT begins 7,9,12,15,17,187,9,12,15,17,18, the gaps 11, 22 and 33 all occur, and 33 occurs only twice (in SS: 7→107\to 10 and 10→1310\to 13); this gives the first statement. Our Walnut computation is an independent check.

5. The Fibonacci word and the Lucas word

Kimberling’s Lucas word ℓ=ℓ0ℓ1⋯=0110011011001100110⋯\boldsymbol{\ell}=\ell_{0}\ell_{1}\cdots=0110011011001100110\cdots (A383422) is the limit of the words s⁡(0)=0s(0)=0, s⁡(1)=011s(1)=011, s⁡(n)=s⁡(n−1)​s​(n−2)s(n)=s(n-1)s(n-2), which have Lucas-number lengths. It is obtained from the Fibonacci word by replacing each 11 by 1111. Indeed, let η\eta be the morphism 0↦00\mapsto 0, 1↦111\mapsto 11, and let t⁡(0)=0t(0)=0, t⁡(1)=01t(1)=01, t⁡(n)=t⁡(n−1)​t​(n−2)t(n)=t(n-1)t(n-2) be the standard prefixes of 𝐟\mathbf{f}, of length Fn+2F_{n+2} with FnF_{n} letters 11. Then η⁡(t⁡(0))=s⁡(0)\eta(t(0))=s(0), η⁡(t⁡(1))=s⁡(1)\eta(t(1))=s(1) and η⁡(t⁡(n))=η⁡(t⁡(n−1))​η​(t⁡(n−2))\eta(t(n))=\eta(t(n-1))\,\eta(t(n-2)), so s⁡(n)=η⁡(t⁡(n))s(n)=\eta(t(n)) for all nn, whence ℓ=η⁡(𝐟)\boldsymbol{\ell}=\eta(\mathbf{f}) and |s⁡(n)|=Fn+2+Fn=Ln+1|s(n)|=F_{n+2}+F_{n}=L_{n+1}.

To express ℓ\boldsymbol{\ell} in Walnut, note that the letter fif_{i} is written at position p⁡(i)=i+ν⁡(i)p(i)=i+\nu(i) of ℓ\boldsymbol{\ell}, where ν⁡(i)=#⁡{j<i:fj=1}\nu(i)=\#\{j<i:f_{j}=1\}. If fi=1f_{i}=1, it also occupies position p⁡(i)+1p(i)+1. The positions of 11 in 𝐟\mathbf{f} are v⁡(n)−1v(n)-1 for n≥1n\geq 1. Hence ν⁡(i)=#⁡{n≥1:v⁡(n)≤i}\nu(i)=\#\{n\geq 1:v(n)\leq i\}, which is the unique q≥0q\geq 0 with v⁡(q)≤i<v⁡(q+1)v(q)\leq i<v(q+1) (with v⁡(0)=0v(0)=0, the case q=0q=0 meaning i<2i<2). This is first-order expressible, so ℓ\boldsymbol{\ell} is Fibonacci-automatic. Walnut confirms that our predicates lw0, lw1 define a word (each position gets exactly one letter) with the correct first 2020 letters.

For (x,y)∈{0,1}2(x,y)\in\{0,1\}^{2} let Px​y={k≥0:fk=x,ℓk=y}P_{xy}=\{k\geq 0:f_{k}=x,\ \ell_{k}=y\}, and let P==P00∪P11P_{=}=P_{00}\cup P_{11}. These are A383423 (P00P_{00}), A383424 (P11P_{11}), A383425 (P01P_{01}), A383426 (P10P_{10}) and A383427 (P=P_{=}).

Theorem 4.

The sets of differences of consecutive elements are:

setOEISgap setP00A383423{1,3,4,5,7}P11A383424{2,3,5,7,8}P01A383425{1,2,3,4,5}P10A383426{3,7,8,10}P=A383427{1,2,3,5,6}\begin{array}[]{lll}\hline\cr\hline\cr\text{set}&\text{OEIS}&\text{gap set}\\ \hline\cr P_{00}&\text{A383423}&\{1,3,4,5,7\}\\ P_{11}&\text{A383424}&\{2,3,5,7,8\}\\ P_{01}&\text{A383425}&\{1,2,3,4,5\}\\ P_{10}&\text{A383426}&\{3,7,8,10\}\\ P_{=}&\text{A383427}&\{1,2,3,5,6\}\\ \hline\cr\hline\cr\end{array}

These are exactly the sets conjectured by Kimberling.

Proof.

Walnut returns TRUE for a383423, …, a383427 in the command file. Removing 77 from the first gap set gives FALSE. ∎

6. Two further conjectures

A003250

Let c⁡(n)=⌊n⁡(5+5)/2⌋=2​n+u⁡(n)c(n)=\left\lfloor n(5+\sqrt{5})/2\right\rfloor=2n+u(n) (A003231), and let A003234 be the set of kk with c⁡(v⁡(k))=v⁡(c⁡(k))−1c(v(k))=v(c(k))-1. A003250 lists, for k∈k\in A003234 in increasing order, the index mm with v⁡(m)=c⁡(k)v(m)=c(k); this is the function zz of Carlitz, Scoville and Vaughan [3]. Schmidt conjectured that m=⌊(3−φ)​k⌋m=\left\lfloor(3-\varphi)k\right\rfloor. In the same entry he recorded the formula m=5​k−1−c⁡(k)m=5k-1-c(k) for k∈k\in A003234, citing Theorems 4.1(ii) and 5.9(vii) of [3]. Since k​φ∉ℤk\varphi\notin\mathbb{Z} for k≥1k\geq 1, we have ⌊(3−φ)​k⌋=3​k−⌈k​φ⌉=3​k−1−u⁡(k)=5​k−1−c⁡(k)\left\lfloor(3-\varphi)k\right\rfloor=3k-\lceil k\varphi\rceil=3k-1-u(k)=5k-1-c(k). So the conjecture is an immediate consequence of those theorems, and we claim nothing new here. As an independent check, Walnut returns TRUE for

Ak $in3234(k) => (Em,x,y $cc(k,x) & $phi2n(m,x) & $phin(k,y) & m+1+y=3*k)

where in3234 is the definition of A003234 and cc that of A003231. This confirms that for every k∈A003234k\in\mathrm{A003234} there is an mm with v⁡(m)=c⁡(k)v(m)=c(k) and m=3​k−1−u⁡(k)m=3k-1-u(k).

A285383

Let μ\mu be the morphism 0↦110\mapsto 11, 1↦011\mapsto 01. Its limiting 00-word is the fixed point 𝐰\mathbf{w} of μ2\mu^{2} that begins with 00. Let 𝐝=1011101010111011⋯\mathbf{d}=1011101010111011\cdots be the period-doubling sequence (A035263), the fixed point of σ:1↦10\sigma:1\mapsto 10, 0↦110\mapsto 11. Mathar conjectured that 𝐰=0​𝐝\mathbf{w}=0\mathbf{d}.

Proposition 5.

𝐰=0​𝐝\mathbf{w}=0\,\mathbf{d}.

Proof.

For each letter aa we have σ⁡(a)=1​ga\sigma(a)=1g_{a} and μ⁡(a)=ga​1\mu(a)=g_{a}1, with g1=0g_{1}=0 and g0=1g_{0}=1. Hence 1​μ​(a)=σ⁡(a)​11\mu(a)=\sigma(a)1, and by induction 1​μ​(u)=σ⁡(u)​11\mu(u)=\sigma(u)1 for every finite word uu. Passing to the limit, 1​μ​(𝐝)=σ⁡(𝐝)=𝐝1\mu(\mathbf{d})=\sigma(\mathbf{d})=\mathbf{d}. Therefore μ⁡(0​𝐝)=11​μ​(𝐝)=1​𝐝\mu(0\mathbf{d})=11\mu(\mathbf{d})=1\mathbf{d}, and μ⁡(1​𝐝)=01​μ​(𝐝)=0​𝐝\mu(1\mathbf{d})=01\mu(\mathbf{d})=0\mathbf{d}. So μ2​(0​𝐝)=0​𝐝\mu^{2}(0\mathbf{d})=0\mathbf{d}. Since 0​𝐝0\mathbf{d} begins with 00, it is the fixed point of μ2\mu^{2} beginning with 00, which is 𝐰\mathbf{w}. ∎
